questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with 45 minutes of crushing central chest pain with sweating and nausea. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Territory-limited ST elevation in the inferior leads with reciprocal change in aVL indicates occlusion of the right coronary artery supplying the inferior wall. Acute pericarditis produces widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression rather than changes confined to one arterial territory. Aortic dissection may cause chest pain but typically gives a widened mediastinum and pulse deficit, not inferior ST elevation.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman reports recurrent episodes of wheeze and breathlessness, worse at night and after colds. She has a history of eczema. Examination reveals a prolonged expiratory phase with bilateral polyphonic wheeze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Episodic, variable airflow obstruction with nocturnal symptoms and an atopic background is characteristic of asthma. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a young non-smoker is unlikely and usually causes a fixed obstruction with a chronic productive cough. Bronchiectasis produces daily purulent sputum and clubbing rather than reversible episodic wheeze.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with three days of black tarry stools and postural dizziness. He has taken ibuprofen regularly for knee pain. Pulse is 105 beats per minute and haemoglobin is 78 g/L. What is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
questions.explanation: Melena with anaemia in a regular NSAID user points to a bleeding peptic ulcer, since NSAIDs impair mucosal prostaglandin-mediated protection. Oesophageal varices require underlying portal hypertension, and this patient has no stigmata of chronic liver disease. A Mallory-Weiss tear typically follows retching and causes haematemesis rather than painless melena.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old with known type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting and abdominal pain. He is drowsy with deep sighing respiration. Capillary glucose is 28 mmol/L and blood ketones are 3.4 mmol/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Marked hyperglycaemia with significant ketonaemia and Kussmaul breathing defines diabetic ketoacidosis, which is precipitated by insulin deficiency and requires fluid and insulin replacement. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state occurs mainly in older type 2 patients, with glucose often above 30 mmol/L and minimal ketosis. Lactic acidosis would show a raised lactate and normal ketones.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with fatigue and heavy menstrual periods. Haemoglobin is 92 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL and serum ferritin 6 mcg/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin in a woman with menorrhagia is diagnostic of iron deficiency, as ferritin reflects depleted iron stores. Thalassaemia trait also causes microcytosis but ferritin is normal or raised and the red cell count is disproportionately high. Vitamin B12 deficiency produces a macrocytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presents with fever, productive cough and rust-coloured sputum. Examination reveals dullness to percussion and bronchial breathing at the right base, and the chest radiograph shows right lower lobe consolidation. Which organism is most likely responsible?
questions.explanation: Lobar consolidation with rusty sputum in an older adult is the classic picture of pneumococcal pneumonia. Mycoplasma usually affects younger adults with bilateral patchy infiltrates and prominent extrapulmonary features such as a bullous myringitis or haemolysis. Pneumocystis causes bilateral interstitial shadowing in immunocompromised patients.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 28 percent is breathless on moderate exertion. He is euvolaemic on ramipril and furosemide. Which additional drug improves survival in this condition?
questions.explanation: Beta blockers such as bisoprolol reduce mortality in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction by blocking sympathetic overactivity and reverse remodelling. Digoxin reduces hospital admissions and symptoms but has not been shown to improve survival. Diltiazem is a negative inotrope and is avoided in systolic heart failure.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an infective exacerbation. He is drowsy and his oxygen saturation is 84 percent breathing air. What oxygen saturation target should be used?
questions.explanation: Patients with COPD at risk of carbon dioxide retention are given controlled oxygen to a target of 88 to 92 percent, because uncontrolled high-flow oxygen can worsen hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis. A target of 94 to 98 percent applies to most other acutely unwell patients but risks over-oxygenation in this group. Saturations below 88 percent risk tissue hypoxia.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with six months of diarrhoea, bloating and weight loss. She has iron deficiency anaemia and an itchy vesicular rash on her elbows. What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.explanation: Chronic diarrhoea with malabsorption, iron deficiency and dermatitis herpetiformis suggests coeliac disease, for which IgA tissue transglutaminase is the recommended screening test, with total IgA checked to exclude deficiency. Faecal calprotectin would point towards inflammatory bowel disease, which does not cause a vesicular rash of the elbows. Duodenal biopsy is used to confirm rather than to screen.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease presents with muscle weakness. Potassium is 6.8 mmol/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves with a widening QRS complex. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: Intravenous calcium gluconate is given first because it stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes and prevents arrhythmia, although it does not lower the serum potassium. Insulin with glucose and nebulised salbutamol shift potassium into cells but act more slowly and do not protect the heart. Sodium bicarbonate has a limited and delayed role.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with weight loss, palpitations and heat intolerance. She has a diffuse smooth goitre, lid lag and fine tremor. Thyroid stimulating hormone is suppressed with a raised free thyroxine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A diffuse goitre with eye signs and suppressed TSH in a young woman is typical of Graves disease, caused by TSH receptor stimulating antibodies. Subacute thyroiditis follows a viral illness, is painful and tender, and does not cause orbitopathy. Toxic multinodular goitre and a toxic adenoma produce a nodular rather than diffuse goitre.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with fatigue and early satiety. He has massive splenomegaly but no lymphadenopathy. The white cell count is 120 x 10^9/L with basophilia, and the Philadelphia chromosome is detected. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome with the BCR-ABL fusion gene is defining for chronic myeloid leukaemia, which characteristically causes massive splenomegaly and basophilia. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia presents with lymphadenopathy and a mature lymphocytosis and lacks this translocation. Primary myelofibrosis causes a leucoerythroblastic picture with tear drop cells and marrow fibrosis.

questions.stem: Four days after an anterior myocardial infarction, a 64-year-old man develops sudden breathlessness and hypotension. There is a new pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, and the chest radiograph shows pulmonary oedema. What is the most likely cause?
options: Free wall rupture with cardiac tamponade
Acute mitral regurgitation due to papillary muscle rupture
questions.explanation: Infarction of the posteromedial papillary muscle leads to acute mitral regurgitation, producing a new apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla with rapid pulmonary oedema and shock. Ventricular septal rupture also causes a new pansystolic murmur but it is loudest at the left sternal edge and often associated with a thrill and right heart failure. Free wall rupture causes tamponade with distended neck veins and pulseless electrical activity rather than a murmur.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness five days after a long-haul flight. Pulse is 118 beats per minute, oxygen saturation is 91 percent and the right calf is swollen. She is normotensive. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.explanation: The combination of recent immobility, unilateral leg swelling, hypoxia and pleuritic pain gives a high clinical probability of pulmonary embolism, so CT pulmonary angiography is the investigation of choice and also allows alternative diagnoses to be assessed. D-dimer is useful only to exclude the diagnosis in low or intermediate probability patients and is non-specific here. Ventilation-perfusion scanning is reserved for patients who cannot receive contrast.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites presents with fever of 38.5 C and generalised abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis shows 480 polymorphonuclear cells per microlitre. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: An ascitic neutrophil count of at least 250 per microlitre defines spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, which is treated with a third-generation cephalosporin such as cefotaxime plus albumin to reduce the risk of hepatorenal syndrome. Oral ciprofloxacin is used for prophylaxis in high-risk patients rather than for established infection. Diuretics and paracentesis do not treat the infection.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man presents with haemoptysis, haematuria and a creatinine that has risen over two weeks. Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies are positive and renal biopsy shows linear IgG deposition along the capillary wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary haemorrhage with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and circulating anti-GBM antibodies indicates anti-GBM disease, and linear immunofluorescence is confirmatory. Granulomatosis with polyangiitis also causes pulmonary-renal syndrome but is ANCA positive with upper airway involvement and pauci-immune crescentic histology. IgA nephropathy usually presents with episodic visible haematuria after a throat infection and has mesangial IgA deposits.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has hypertension that remains uncontrolled on three agents. Potassium is 2.9 mmol/L with a metabolic alkalosis. Plasma aldosterone is high and plasma renin activity is suppressed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Resistant hypertension with hypokalaemia, alkalosis, high aldosterone and suppressed renin is the biochemical signature of primary hyperaldosteronism, usually from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia. Renal artery stenosis causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with a raised renin level. Phaeochromocytoma produces paroxysmal symptoms with raised catecholamines rather than this aldosterone profile.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has a CD4 count of 60 cells per microlitre. He reports three weeks of dry cough and progressive exertional breathlessness. Oxygen saturation is 88 percent on air and high resolution CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Subacute dry cough, progressive hypoxia and bilateral perihilar ground-glass change in a patient with a CD4 count below 200 cells per microlitre is typical of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, treated with high dose co-trimoxazole and corticosteroids when hypoxic. Bacterial pneumonia has an acute onset with focal consolidation and purulent sputum. Pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma produces nodules and pleural effusion, often with cutaneous lesions.
